# Part V: Inference and Serving {#part-inference .unnumbered}

> "large online services need to create a predictably responsive whole out of
> less predictable parts."
>
> Jeffrey Dean and Luiz Andre Barroso, ["The Tail at Scale"](https://research.google/pubs/the-tail-at-scale/)

Training produces weights. A service has to turn those weights into tokens on a
clock, for many users, at a price someone can pay. Inference is not a smaller
version of training. It has a different shape: prefill and decode, compute and
memory, latency and throughput, one request and the batch it must share.

@sec-serving-problem names the core tension: a generated token is cheap in FLOPs
and expensive in memory movement, and the key-value cache grows exactly where the
service wishes it would not. Once that is the problem, the cache becomes a resource
to be scheduled, and @sec-memory-scheduling treats it as one, with paging, prefix
sharing, batching, and phase splitting. The next two sections push on the expensive
step itself: @sec-faster-decoding looks for ways to get more than one token out of
it, while @sec-quantization-kernels shrinks the bytes and changes the kernels so the
hardware spends less time moving matrices around. Last, @sec-structured-long-context
and @sec-serving-multimodal show two ways the neat text-serving problem becomes less
neat: the output may be constrained by a schema, the context may be long enough to
need pruning, or the input may include visual tokens the tokenizer never made.

Read this part as a study of the word afford. A model that is impressive but too
slow, too memory-hungry, or too hard to batch is not yet infrastructure. Serving
is the layer that turns capability into something repeatable, and it is also the
layer that pushes back into model design.
